newsitem.title: CROATIA: Court says Bosnian Croat warlord must stay in jail.
newsitem.headline: Court says Bosnian Croat warlord must stay in jail.

text.p: Croatia's constitutional court ruled that a Bosnian Croat warlord arrested last month should remain in custody until an investigation against him is completed, state news agency HINA said on Wednesday.
The court brushed off a complaint by Mladen Naletilic, better known as "Tuta", against a Zagreb municipal court's decision to keep him incarcerated pending inquiry results.

"Naletilic's suit was illegal as it was launched before all other legal possibilities were exhausted," it said in a statment, adding he could file a constitutional suit only after criminal proceedings against him were completed.

Naletilic, arrested in February in a village near Croatia's border with southwest Bosnia, is believed by Western diplomats and human rights monitors to be the paramount paramilitary mafia leader in the divided Bosnian city of Mostar.

His capture, coinciding with arrests of his right-hand man Vinko Martinovic and several other Mostar Croats, was hailed as the start of a crackdown on organised crime in Mostar which has victimised minority Moslems.

Naletilic and Martinovic have been accused by Western mediators of being at the centre of a gangster cartel that runs western, Croat-controlled Mostar and opposes international efforts to reunite the city.

The captures were seen as a policy turnabout for Croatia, whose authorities have in the past appeared to tolerate, if not protect, rogue elements in Bosnia's Herzegovina region who oppose normalising relations with Bosnian Moslems.

But a month later Naletilic has still not been officially indicted, nor have charges against him been made public, raising suspicions that his arrest was staged to appease Western critics until their attentions are drawn elsewhere.
Independent Croatian weeklies Globus and Nacional said this week he would be indicted for abduction and murder of a man by his paramilitaries in southern Herzegovina in 1993.

Both weeklies, quoting unnamed sources close to Naletilic, reported he had tuberculosis and had been transferred to a prison hospital on the outskirts of Zagreb. Neither claim could be independently confirmed.
